title: Integration by substitution
section: Techniques of Integration ▷ Integration by Substitution
terms: u-substitution; change of variable; reverse chain rule; transformed limits.

exposition.text:

Substitution reverses the chain rule: f(g(x))g (x) dx = F(g(x)) + C when F = f . Set u = g(x)
′
and du = g (x)dx; rewrite the entire integrand in the new variable. For definite integrals, use
corresponding limits u = g(a) and u = g(b), or first return to the original variable before
applying the original limits.
Look for an inner expression whose derivative occurs elsewhere in the integrand. Completing a
square, factoring, or a trigonometric identity may reveal the pattern. Do not leave a mixture of
x and u without an explicit relation. A substitution that is not one-to-one can still implement
the chain-rule identity when used correctly; geometric changes of variable may require splitting
branches.

solution.text:
2
The chain-rule antiderivative is sin(x ), with equal endpoint values. Hence the integral is
zero. Substitution sends both oriented endpoints to u = 1, correctly giving zero; injectivity
is not required for this reverse-chain-rule identity. Oddness independently verifies the
result.

(A) 1 (B) 2 (C) 3 (D) 6 (E) 18

solution.text:
2
Set u = 1 + 3x , so du = 6x dx and the endpoints become 1 and 4. The desired integral is
one sixth of the given integral, hence 1. No formula for f or its antiderivative is needed.
